title: How to Read This Graph
oneLineScope: How this graph is organized, the edge-type legend, and where to start.
prose:
This tutorial covers transformers and how the first large language models were trained — from the Attention Is All You Need paper (Vaswani et al., 2017) through the GPT family and the scaling-law results of Kaplan et al. (2020), with a brief terminal bridge to supervised fine-tuning and the earliest instruction-tuned models. It is not a survey of frontier systems or a review of the last five years of architecture variations. The bargain is depth over breadth: twenty nodes, each long enough to give you the intuition and the mathematics to make the connections yourself, each tethered to primary and expository sources so you can go deeper anywhere and trust what you integrate.

A graph, not a book

The material is organized as a directed graph, not a linear sequence of chapters. That reflects how the ideas actually hang together: some nodes are strict prerequisites for others; some stand as siblings that reward direct comparison; some exist mainly to set up what follows. Reading it linearly would bury the contrasts and conceal the architecture of the field. Reading it freely, with the map in front of you, lets you navigate by interest and follow threads rather than march through a table of contents.

There are three kinds of edge, drawn distinctly in the map below:

  • Prerequisite (solid arrow): understand the source node before the target. These form the backbone path through the material. If a node's explanation assumes a concept, that concept is a prerequisite.
  • Leads-to (orange arrow): the source sets up the target as the natural next topic in the narrative arc, but the connection is motivational rather than strictly logical. You can enter the target independently; the source enriches it.
  • Contrast (dashed line, undirected): the two nodes are conceptual siblings worth examining side by side. The encoder/decoder fork in this graph — autoregressive LM, masked LM, and the encoder–decoder contrast node — is the main cluster of contrast edges.

Two entry points

The graph has two recommended starting points, both marked on the map.

Distributional semantics (node 02) is the on-ramp for the conceptually minded — specifically, for anyone coming from the Firth/Harris tradition of meaning-from-context that underpins corpus linguistics and early computational semantics. If the idea that a word's meaning can be recovered from its distributional environment is native to you, this node bridges directly from that intuition to the dense learned representations that power the transformer. The path from there follows: distributional semantics leads to word embeddings, which is a prerequisite for scaled dot-product attention.

Scaled dot-product attention (node 06) is the entry point for the impatient — for anyone who wants to get to the core mechanism first and fill in the conceptual prehistory afterward. Attention is the operation the transformer is built around; every other architectural choice is, at bottom, infrastructure for running attention at scale. If you know what soft, learned alignment looks like from statistical machine translation (IBM models, HMM-based alignment), you already have most of the intuition, and this node will feel like coming home.

Neither path is mandatory. The map is there for you to wander. Follow prerequisite edges when the dependencies matter; follow leads-to edges when you want the narrative; hop contrast edges when you want to compare siblings directly.

The shape of the journey

Working left to right across the graph map: the first phase is prehistory and foundations — the distributional and connectionist ideas that the transformer draws on, the recurrent models it replaced, and the soft-alignment work in neural machine translation that directly anticipated the attention mechanism. The second phase is the core attention machinery: the scaled dot-product operation, multi-head attention, and positional encoding. The third phase is architecture assembly: the residual-and-norm transformer block, the full encoder–decoder stack, and then the fork into decoder-only (GPT lineage) and encoder-only (BERT) variants. The fourth phase is training mechanics: tokenization and subword vocabularies, pretraining objectives, and optimization at scale. The fifth and final phase is scaling and the bridge: data and compute, scaling laws as a quantitative framework, in-context learning as a behavior that emerges at scale, and a brief terminal node on supervised fine-tuning and the step toward instruction-following models.

The bibliography

Every node carries a short annotated bibliography in two tiers. Primary sources are the original research papers: they are the authority for the exact claims, and the annotations point you to the specific section or equation that serves each point. Exposition sources are secondary texts chosen for teaching quality, not merely citation count. Progress and visited state are tracked in the current session only; they reset when you close the document. That is by design — the graph is meant to be re-entered, not finished once and archived.

bibliography.citation: Vaswani, A., Shazeer, N., Parmar, N., Uszkoreit, J., Jones, L., Gomez, A. N., Kaiser, Ł., & Polosukhin, I. (2017). Attention Is All You Need. NeurIPS.
bibliography.annotation: The anchor paper for this entire tutorial. §1 motivates the architecture; §3 defines scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, and positional encoding; §5 gives the training recipe. Return to it often — it is short, dense, and precise.

bibliography.citation: Jurafsky, D., & Martin, J. H. (3rd ed., draft). Speech and Language Processing. Chapters 6–11.
bibliography.annotation: The standard graduate-level NLP textbook, freely available. Chapters 6–7 cover vector semantics and embeddings (bridging from distributional semantics); chapters 9–11 cover RNNs, attention, and transformers with careful notation. Good companion for any node in the prehistory and architecture phases.
